In the Mond process it is first reduced with hydrogen (water gas) at about 400 C.
This powder has a very active surface and combines readily with carbon monoxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_nickel.plac: Approximation: reduction temperature is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.carbon_monoxide_g: A gas with no colour or smell that is very harmful.

2 coke + a bag of oxygen make 2 (burned with little oxygen). Material for nickel carbonyl and the Reppe process. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled, category 3), flammable gas, reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
2C + O2 -> 2CO. It binds to haemoglobin in blood over 200 times more strongly than oxygen, so blood cannot carry oxygen.
Burning charcoal or coal in a closed room causes carbon monoxide poisoning; homes now have alarms for it.
Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The gas producer is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel_carbonyl_g: Nickel joined with carbon monoxide into a gas. Highly toxic. If you carry it, some may leak and make you feel ill.

Crude nickel + 4 bags of carbon monoxide (about 50 C). Decompose in a furnace (about 200 C) for nickel. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhaled, category 2), carcinogenic (category 1B), reproductive toxicity, flammable. Treated only as an industrial material.
Ni + 4CO -> Ni(CO)4 (about 50 C); Ni(CO)4 -> Ni + 4CO (about 200 C). Iron and copper do not become gases at these temperatures, so only nickel is taken out.

In 1890 Mond and his team found it while studying why nickel valves corroded in carbon monoxide. A metal turning into a gas was a great surprise. Because it is so toxic, plants keep it strictly away from air.
Approximation: the carbon monoxide released on decomposition is not recovered (really it is reused). Leaks do not use up the bag.
message.semiconductor-lab.nickel_carbony: Nickel carbonyl leaked. Headache and weakness (highly toxic)
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note1: A silvery-white metal that resists rust. Found in coins and stainless steel.
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note2: Decompose nickel carbonyl in a furnace (Mond process, very pure). + aluminium -> Raney nickel precursor (catalyst, [2-51]). ⚠ GHS: skin sensitizer, suspected carcinogen (category 2).
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note3: Like iron and cobalt, it sticks to magnets. It soaks up hydrogen readily, so it catalyzes reactions that add hydrogen (hydrogenation).
item.semiconductor-lab.nickel.note4: In 1897 Sabatier found that nickel catalyzes adding hydrogen to oils and unsaturated compounds (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1912). Margarine is made with this reaction.
item.semiconductor-lab.rock_crystal.note: Quartz grown into a large clear crystal. A curious stone that makes electricity when squeezed.
A rare drop from quartz veins mined without silk touch. Cut it with a diamond saw for quartz blanks.

In 1880 the Curie brothers (Pierre and Jacques) found that squeezing quartz produces electric charge on its surface (piezoelectricity). Conversely, a voltage makes the crystal stretch or shrink slightly.
Brazil was the big source of natural quartz, and radio crystals ran short in World War II, which led to synthetic quartz [8-18].
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note1: An iron plate with holes that get smaller step by step. Pull a metal rod through them in turn and it becomes a thin wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note2: Crafting: 3 iron ingots + 1 flint → 1 (the flint pierces the holes). Gold ingot + draw plate → 8 gold wire; copper ingot + draw plate → 8 copper wire. The plate comes back (not used up).
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note3: Going through a hole, the metal gets as much longer as it gets thinner (the volume stays the same). Too big a step snaps it, so it is pulled through dozens of slightly smaller holes.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.note4: Wire was pulled by hand from ancient times; in 14th-century Nuremberg water power took over (⚠️ the date is uncertain). Roebling's 1893 stranding machine twisted steel wires into suspension-bridge ropes.
item.semiconductor-lab.draw_plate.placeh: Approximation: the graded holes are one plate and drawing is done at the crafting table. The tool is not used up.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note1: A diamond with a tiny hole through it. It can draw very thin wire.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note2: Crafting: 1 diamond + 1 iron ingot (mount) → 1. Gold wire + diamond die → 8 gold bonding wire. The die comes back.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note3: Holes in an iron plate wear wider, but a diamond hole hardly wears, so even wire finer than a hair stays the same thickness.
item.semiconductor-lab.diamond_die.note4: Light-bulb tungsten wire and chip gold wire (about 25 µm) are drawn through diamond dies. ⚠️ When diamond dies became common is not yet checked.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note1: Gold wire drawn through a draw plate.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note2: Gold ingot + draw plate → 8. Drawn again through a diamond die it becomes fine gold bonding wire for chips.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note3: Gold is soft and extremely ductile: a gram can be drawn into kilometres of wire. It never rusts, so it suits electrical contacts.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_wire.note4: Hammered gold leaf gets as thin as about 0.1 µm.
item.semiconductor-lab.gold_bonding_wire: Gold wire a third as thick as a hair. It connects a chip to the outside leads.
Gold wire + diamond die → 8 (about 25 µm across). The wire bonder [9-33] joins chip pads to header leads with it (one wire per pad).
Gold does not rust and sticks to aluminium pads under heat and pressure, so it was chosen to wire up chips.
Cheaper copper wire is common today, but it is harder to bond (copper oxidises and is harder).
Approximation: thickness is not modelled. One wire = one pad.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note1: Copper wire drawn through a draw plate. The core of electric cables.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note2: Copper ingot + draw plate → 8. Few uses yet (cable cores, submarine cable [15-03]).
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note3: Copper conducts electricity second only to silver and is cheap and ductile, so almost all wiring is copper.
item.semiconductor-lab.copper_wire.note4: Copper wire is made by pulling a thick rod through small holes dozens of times.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern_under_hcl: Bittern set up to be dried together with hydrogen chloride gas.
2 bittern + a bag of hydrogen chloride. Dry it in a furnace for anhydrous magnesium chloride. ⚠ Hydrogen chloride is corrosive and toxic (GHS).
Simply heating MgCl2·6H2O makes it react with its own water into MgO and hydrogen chloride (hydrolysis). Surrounding it with hydrogen chloride holds that back so only the water leaves.
Dow worked out ways around this difficult drying step.
Approximation: the number of drying stages is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.anhydrous_magnesi: Magnesium chloride with no water at all. Melt it and pass electricity to get magnesium.
Dry bittern under hydrogen chloride in a furnace. Magnesium cell -> magnesium + chlorine. Also recovered from the Kroll process [1-41].
MgCl2. Melts at about 710 C. In molten salt the ions can move, so it conducts (molten-salt electrolysis).
Any water left forms MgO during electrolysis and fouls the cell.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_oxide.n: A white powder you get by roasting bittern as it is. No magnesium can be taken from it.
Roast bittern in a furnace (without hydrogen chloride). Experiment: compare with drying under hydrogen chloride.
Magnesia does not melt even at 2800 C, so it lines furnaces as magnesia brick.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_oxide.p: Approximation: intermediate basic chlorides are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium.note1: A very light silvery metal. It burns with a blinding white light.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium.note2: Made in the magnesium cell. The reducing agent that takes titanium out in the Kroll process [1-41]. ⚠ GHS: flammable solid, reacts with water releasing hydrogen (powder is especially dangerous).
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium.note3: Density 1.74 g/cm3 (two-thirds of aluminium). It burns to MgO with an intense white light (old photo flashes) and water cannot put it out.
item.semiconductor-lab.magnesium.note4: A litre of seawater holds about 1.3 g of magnesium. From 1941 Dow extracted magnesium from seawater in the USA; it went into WWII aircraft.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_cell.n: A cell that takes magnesium out of molten salt with electricity.
6 steel + graphite rod (anode) + copper cable. 10 kW. 1 anhydrous magnesium chloride -> 1 magnesium + 1 bag of chlorine (20 s).
Cathode: Mg2+ + 2e- -> Mg (light, it floats); anode: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-. The chlorine is turned back into hydrochloric acid and reused.
Dow began making it from Michigan brine in 1916 and from seawater in Texas in 1941.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_cell.p: Approximation: about 700 C and the voltage are not given as numbers.
item.semiconductor-lab.ilmenite.note1: Black grains mixed in with iron sand. The source of titanium.
item.semiconductor-lab.ilmenite.note2: Sometimes (10%) comes up with iron sand when you dig it. + charcoal + 3 bags of chlorine -> crude titanium tetrachloride.
item.semiconductor-lab.ilmenite.note3: FeTiO3, an oxide of iron and titanium. Less magnetic than magnetite.
item.semiconductor-lab.ilmenite.note4: In 1791 Gregor, a British clergyman, found a new element in black grains ('menachanite') in Cornish sand.
item.semiconductor-lab.ilmenite.placehol: Approximation: the drop chance from iron sand is a game value.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_titanium_te: A yellowish liquid with iron chloride mixed in. Distil it to clean it.

Ilmenite + charcoal + 3 chlorine. + quartz still (returned) -> titanium tetrachloride. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, acute toxicity (inhaled). Gives off white hydrogen chloride smoke in moist air. Treated only as an industrial material.
Much titanium white (TiO2 pigment) is still made by this chloride process.
Approximation: iron chloride and carbon monoxide are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.titanium_tetrachl: A clear liquid that smokes white in air. Raw material for titanium and for polyethylene catalysts.

Distil crude titanium tetrachloride. + 2 magnesium + argon -> Kroll charge. Also used for the Ziegler-Natta catalyst [2-50]. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, acute toxicity (inhaled). Reacts violently with water. Treated only as an industrial material.
TiCl4, boiling point 136 C. Distillation separates it from iron chloride and others with different boiling points.
It reacts with moisture into dense white smoke of TiO2 and hydrogen chloride, once used for naval smokescreens and skywriting.
item.semiconductor-lab.kroll_charge.note: Titanium tetrachloride and magnesium sealed in air-free argon. Fired, it yields titanium.
Titanium tetrachloride + 2 magnesium + a bag of argon. Furnace (about 800-900 C) -> sponge with salt.
TiCl4 + 2Mg -> Ti + 2MgCl2. Hot titanium reacts readily with oxygen and nitrogen, so it is done in argon.
In 1940 Wilhelm Kroll of Luxembourg devised this method, making industrial titanium possible.
item.semiconductor-lab.kroll_charge.plac: Approximation: the steel vessel and temperature are not modelled.
A porous lump of titanium soaked with magnesium chloride.
Fire the Kroll charge in a furnace. + quartz still (vacuum distillation, returned) -> titanium sponge. Magnesium chloride stays in the grid (back to Mg and chlorine in the magnesium cell [1-39]).
Magnesium chloride evaporates more easily than titanium, so heating in a vacuum drives off just the salt.
Magnesium and chlorine go round and round and are used again and again (the Kroll cycle).
Approximation: vacuum distillation is represented by the still.
item.semiconductor-lab.titanium_sponge.n: Titanium like a sponge full of holes. A light, strong metal that does not rust.
Vacuum-distil the sponge with salt. Material for vacuum pumps and optics ([5-08], [7-21]).
Density 4.5 g/cm3 (about 60% of iron) yet as strong as steel. A thin oxide skin keeps it from rusting.
Used for aircraft frames, artificial bones and teeth, and spectacle frames. To make ingots it is remelted in a vacuum (vacuum arc remelting).
item.semiconductor-lab.titanium_sponge.p: Approximation: vacuum arc remelting into ingots is not implemented.
item.semiconductor-lab.cadmium.note1: A soft silvery metal found in small amounts in zinc ore. It is poisonous, so it is used only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.cadmium.note2: 6 zinc oxide + 2 charcoal + quartz still (returned). Material for the Weston standard cell. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, carcinogen, health hazard, aquatic hazard.
item.semiconductor-lab.cadmium.note3: Discovered in 1817 by Stromeyer in Germany, in zinc carbonate. When zinc is distilled, cadmium, with its lower boiling point, comes off first.
item.semiconductor-lab.cadmium.note4: Itai-itai disease along the Jinzu River in Toyama, Japan, was caused by cadmium washed down from a mine upstream (recognised in 1968 as Japan's first official pollution disease). It damaged kidneys and bones, and many people suffered for years. Since then cadmium has been dropped from many uses.
item.semiconductor-lab.cadmium.placehold: Approximation: the cadmium content of zinc (real: 0.1-0.5%) and the distillation are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite.note1: A black stone that blackens your hands. It goes inside dry cells.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite.note2: Dropped by pyrolusite ore in shallow stone. Zinc + 2 of this + ammonium chloride + graphite rod -> 2 dry cells.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite.note3: MnO2. In a dry cell it turns hydrogen at the positive (carbon) side into water, so bubbles do not build up and weaken the current (polarization) - a 'depolarizer'. It was once used to decolorize glass too.
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite.note4: Most manganese ores are layers laid down on old sea or lake floors, where dissolved manganese joined with oxygen. Early Leclanché cells used crushed natural pyrolusite; modern cells use purer electrolytic MnO2 (EMD).
item.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite.placeh: Approximation: in the game it is an ore in shallow stone (real deposits are sedimentary layers or oxidized zones).
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrolusite_ore.n: Stone with black grains. Mine it for pyrolusite.
In shallow Overworld stone (height 0 to 96). Mine it with a pickaxe.
An ore of manganese dioxide MnO2. Manganese also makes steel tougher ([1-63]).
The deep sea floor is littered with 'manganese nodules', lumps of manganese that grew like pearls.
block.semiconductor-lab.spodumene_ore.no: Stone with whitish crystals inside granite. The source of lithium.
A rare ore found only in granite (rarer than cassiterite). Mine it with a pickaxe for spodumene.
It forms in pegmatite - coarse-crystal rock that is the last part of a granite magma to freeze, where lithium, tin, tantalum and others gather.
Pegmatite crystals can grow huge: in South Dakota, spodumene crystals over ten metres long were found.
block.semiconductor-lab.spodumene_ore.pl: Approximation: in the game it is an ore in granite (real ore is pegmatite veins). Most lithium today comes from salt-lake brine, but vanilla has no salt lakes, so only the ore route.
item.semiconductor-lab.spodumene.note1: A stone containing lithium. As it is, acid hardly dissolves it.
item.semiconductor-lab.spodumene.note2: Roast it in a blast furnace to change it into a form (beta) that dissolves easily.
item.semiconductor-lab.spodumene.note3: LiAlSi2O6, a mineral of lithium, aluminium, silicon and oxygen.
item.semiconductor-lab.spodumene.note4: Lithium was found in 1817 by Arfwedson in Berzelius's lab in Sweden, in another mineral, petalite. It was named from the Greek word for 'stone'.
item.semiconductor-lab.beta_spodumene.no: Stone that has been roasted so acid can dissolve it.
Made by roasting spodumene in a blast furnace. 2 + sulfuric acid + water -> lithium sulfate (bottle and bucket returned).
At about 1050 °C the crystal changes its arrangement (alpha -> beta) and swells, full of gaps. Sulfuric acid soaks in and turns the lithium into lithium sulfate, which dissolves in water.
The unroasted alpha form is hard and barely dissolves even in sulfuric acid. Just changing the crystal shape with heat changes how easily it dissolves.
item.semiconductor-lab.beta_spodumene.pl: Approximation: a blast furnace instead of a rotary kiln at about 1050 °C. Acid roasting (about 250 °C), water leaching and the aluminosilicate residue are left out.
item.semiconductor-lab.lithium_sulfate.n: Lithium dissolved in water, dried into a white powder.
2 roasted spodumene + sulfuric acid + water. + soda ash -> lithium carbonate.
Li2SO4. Unlike sodium or potassium sulfate, it gets less soluble as the water gets hotter.
Lithium compounds colour a flame red (flame test), which Bunsen and Kirchhoff's spectroscope also showed.
item.semiconductor-lab.lithium_carbonate: A white lithium powder. A material for batteries.
Lithium sulfate + soda ash. A material for the lithium-ion battery cathode (planned).
Li2SO4 + Na2CO3 -> Li2CO3 + Na2SO4. Lithium carbonate hardly dissolves in hot water, so it settles out.
Metallic lithium was first made in 1855 by Bunsen and Matthiessen by electrolysing molten lithium chloride. It is so light it floats on water.
Approximation: settling in hot water, filtering and the sodium sulfate by-product are left out. There is no metallic lithium yet.
block.semiconductor-lab.tantalite_ore.no: Granite with heavy black crystals. The source of tantalum.
A very rare ore found only in granite (rarer than spodumene). Mining it with a pickaxe gives tantalite.
The last part of a granite magma to freeze (pegmatite) gathers lithium, tin, tantalum and more.
Much tantalum ore comes from central Africa and funded wars (conflict minerals). Buyers must now check where it comes from.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalite.note1: A heavy black oxide mineral of iron, manganese, tantalum and niobium.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalite.note2: Tantalum refinery: with 2 hydrofluoric acid + 1 potassium fluoride → K2TaF7 (Marignac process).
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalite.note3: (Fe,Mn)(Ta,Nb)2O6. Tantalum and niobium are so alike that chemists argued for over 40 years whether they were the same element.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalite.note4: Ekeberg found tantalum in 1802. It is named after Tantalus of Greek myth, who could never drink the water around him, because it does not dissolve in acids.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_fluorot: White crystals of tantalum, fluorine and potassium. Tantalum is extracted from them.
Tantalum refinery: heat with metallic sodium → tantalum.
It dissolves poorly, so it crystallises out of the HF solution while the near-identical niobium salt (K2NbOF5) stays dissolved; this first separated the two (Marignac, 1866).
Still the main industrial feedstock for tantalum, and sodium reduction has been used for over a century.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium.note1: A silvery metal soft enough to cut with a knife. It burns on contact with water, so it is sealed in an iron container.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium.note2: Castner cell: 4 sodium hydroxide + empty iron flask → this. Used to reduce tantalum (the flask comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium.note3: 4NaOH → 4Na + O2 + 2H2O (electrolysis of molten NaOH). A very strong reducing agent that frees metals from their fluorides and chlorides.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium.note4: Davy first isolated it in 1807; the Castner process of 1886 made it cheap (for making aluminium). It reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen (GHS: water-reactive flammable gas, corrosive).
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium.placeholde: Omitted: ⚠️ the real Castner process is only about half efficient (water formed reacts with the sodium). Amounts are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalum.note1: A heavy metal that hardly melts or corrodes. A thin layer goes under a chip's copper wiring.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalum.note2: Tantalum refinery: K2TaF7 + metallic sodium → this. Used as a sputtering target for the barrier under copper wiring.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalum.note3: Melts at about 3000 °C. Its oxide skin is so tough that acids cannot attack it, and that oxide makes small high-capacity capacitors.
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalum.note4: In 1903 von Bolton at Siemens & Halske made ductile tantalum, and tantalum-filament lamps went on sale in 1905 (carbon → tantalum → tungsten).
item.semiconductor-lab.tantalum.placehol: Omitted: ⚠️ the reduced powder is really melted in vacuum to make ductile metal. Niobium is not made.
block.semiconductor-lab.castner_cell.not: Passes current through molten sodium hydroxide to free metallic sodium.
2 kW. 4 sodium hydroxide + empty iron flask → metallic sodium (in the flask, 20 s).
NaOH is melted at about 320 °C in an iron pot with a nickel anode and an iron cathode. Sodium floats up at the cathode and is skimmed off.
Castner invented it in 1886 to make sodium cheap for aluminium production (soon replaced by the Hall–Héroult process, but sodium found other uses).
block.semiconductor-lab.castner_cell.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ power, time and efficiency are game values. Oxygen and water are discarded.
gui.semiconductor-lab.castner_cell.need_: Needs 4 NaOH and an iron flask
block.semiconductor-lab.tantalum_refiner: Extracts tantalum from tantalite. What you put in picks the step.
3 kW, 20 s each. ① 1 tantalite + 2 hydrofluoric acid + 1 potassium fluoride → K2TaF7 (acid containers come back) ② K2TaF7 + metallic sodium → tantalum (the iron flask comes back).
① Marignac process: K2TaF7 crystallises while niobium stays in solution. ② K2TaF7 + 5Na → Ta + 2KF + 5NaF in an iron pot; the salts are washed away.
Hydrofluoric acid reaches into bone, so it is used only as an industrial material, in lead or polyethylene containers (GHS: skull, corrosive). The tank is lead-lined.
Omitted: ⚠️ the niobium liquor and washed salts are discarded. Power, time and amounts are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenite.note1: A soft silvery ore that looks just like graphite. It comes up as a by-product of copper mines.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenite.note2: Mining copper ore rarely (5%) gives it. Roasting in the reverberatory furnace gives molybdenum trioxide + sulfur dioxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenite.note3: In 1778 Scheele in Sweden showed it was neither graphite (carbon) nor a lead ore, and extracted the oxide of a new element. The name molybdenum comes from the Greek for lead.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenite.note4: MoS2 forms layered crystals that slide like graphite, so it is still used as a lubricant. Most molybdenum today is a by-product of porphyry copper mines.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenite.place: Approximation: the drop rate (5%) is a game value.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenum_trioxi: A pale powder made by roasting molybdenite in air.
Molybdenite roasted in the reverberatory furnace (2MoS2 + 7O2 -> 2MoO3 + 4SO2). Reduced in the hydrogen furnace to molybdenum. ⚠ GHS: health hazard (do not inhale).
In 1781 Hjelm reduced it with carbon and obtained metallic molybdenum for the first time.
MoO3 sublimes easily around 700 C. Industry reduces roasted concentrate with hydrogen in two stages to molybdenum powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenum.note1: A silvery metal that hardly melts even at very high temperatures. It goes into EUV mirrors.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenum.note2: Molybdenum trioxide + 3 hydrogen bags in the hydrogen furnace (3 kW, 30 s). Stacked alternately with silicon on ULE glass in the vacuum evaporator, it makes a multilayer mirror.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenum.note3: It melts at about 2620 C. It strengthens stainless and tool steels and was used in lamp and vacuum-tube parts.
item.semiconductor-lab.molybdenum.note4: For 13.5 nm EUV light, molybdenum and silicon differ strongly in refractive index and absorb little, so layers with a period of about 7 nm reflect strongly.
item.semiconductor-lab.zircon.note1: Small brown or red grains in beach sand. A very hard, very lasting mineral.
item.semiconductor-lab.zircon.note2: Rarely (5%) found when digging iron sand on beaches (the same heavy sand as ilmenite). + 2 sodium hydroxide + water -> crude zirconia.
item.semiconductor-lab.zircon.note3: ZrSiO4. It always carries hafnium, about 2% of the zirconium (almost the same size, so they swap places in the crystal).
item.semiconductor-lab.zircon.note4: Zircon lasts so long that grains about 4.4 billion years old have been found in Australia - the oldest pieces of Earth's minerals.
item.semiconductor-lab.zircon.placeholde: Approximation: really separated from beach heavy-mineral sand (ilmenite, rutile, zircon). In the game a by-product of iron sand.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_zirconia.no: White powder from zircon with the silicon removed. Hafnium is still in it.
Zircon + 2 sodium hydroxide + water. + 2 hydrofluoric acid + potassium fluoride -> crude potassium fluorozirconate.
Fusing zircon with sodium hydroxide (caustic fusion) turns the silicon into sodium silicate, which dissolves in water, leaving zirconium and hafnium as oxides.
Zirconia also makes ceramic knives and cubic zirconia, a diamond-like gem.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_zirconia.pl: Approximation: really fused above about 600 °C. In the game, a crafting table (heating left out).
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_fluorozirco: Crystals with zirconium and hafnium mixed. Dissolve and recrystallize again and again to separate them.

Crude zirconia + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + potassium fluoride. 8 + water: fractional crystallization -> 1 potassium fluorohafnate, and pure potassium fluorozirconate stays in each of the 8 slots.
K2ZrF6 and K2HfF6 are nearly identical but dissolve slightly differently (the hafnium salt more easily). Dissolving, cooling and crystallizing dozens of times gathers the hafnium in the liquid.
In 1924 Hevesy and coworkers first collected hafnium by repeating this fractional crystallization. Today solvent extraction with organic liquids is used.
Approximation: dozens of recrystallizations are merged into one. Real hafnium is about 2%, so 1 from 8 is generous.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_fluoroz: White zirconium crystals with the hafnium removed.
Left over from fractional crystallization. + 2 sodium (iron flasks returned) -> crude zirconium.
K2ZrF6. Sodium takes the fluorine and leaves zirconium metal (how Berzelius made the first zirconium metal in 1824).
Nuclear fuel is clad in zirconium alloy because it barely absorbs neutrons. Hafnium absorbs them strongly, so it must be removed thoroughly.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_fluoroh: 8 crude potassium fluorozirconate + water (fractional crystallization). + ammonia water -> hafnium hydroxide. + 2 sodium -> crude hafnium.
K2HfF6. Its chemistry is almost the same as zirconium's, so nobody noticed it for a long time.
In 1923 Coster and Hevesy in Copenhagen found new lines in the X-ray spectrum of zircon and so discovered hafnium, named after Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_hydroxide: A white hafnium precipitate. Roast it to get hafnium oxide.
Potassium fluorohafnate + ammonia water (bottle returned). Roast in a furnace -> hafnium oxide.
Made alkaline with ammonia, insoluble Hf(OH)4 settles out. Roasting drives off the water, leaving HfO2.
Roasting drives off water and lowers the weight; from the change you can calculate what was there (gravimetric analysis).
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_oxide.not: A white powder that hardly melts. The thin insulating film in today's chip transistors.
Roast hafnium hydroxide in a furnace. The material for gate insulators (high-k) in FinFETs and others.
HfO2 stores electric charge (dielectric constant) about 5 times better than SiO2. The film can be thicker for the same effect, cutting the current that tunnels through a too-thin SiO2 film.
In 2007, with Intel's 45 nm chips, the gate insulator changed from SiO2 to hafnium-based high-k. Real films are grown one atomic layer at a time by ALD (alternating hafnium tetrachloride and water).
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_zirconium.n: Dark metal powder still mixed with oxygen and others.
Potassium fluorozirconate + 2 sodium. + iodine + tungsten wire -> zirconium crystal bar.
Zirconium readily takes up oxygen and nitrogen, which makes it brittle.
Powdered zirconium burns easily in air and was once used in camera flashes. ⚠ GHS: flammable solid (powder).
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_hafnium.not: Dark metal powder still mixed with oxygen and others.
Potassium fluorohafnate + 2 sodium. + iodine + tungsten wire -> hafnium crystal bar.
Like zirconium, it readily takes up oxygen and nitrogen.
item.semiconductor-lab.zirconium_bar.not: A bar of very pure zirconium, its surface knobbly with crystals.
Crude zirconium + iodine + tungsten wire (iodide process).

Warmed with iodine, the crude metal turns into gaseous zirconium iodide ZrI4. On a red-hot tungsten wire it splits: pure zirconium builds up on the wire and the iodine goes back to carry more metal. Oxygen and nitrogen do not form gases with iodine, so they stay behind.
Devised in 1925 by van Arkel and de Boer in the Netherlands (iodide or crystal bar process). It is still used to make very pure metals.
item.semiconductor-lab.zirconium_bar.pla: Approximation: the vacuum vessel, heating the wire to about 1400 °C and days of growth are left out. Iodine is reused in the real process but one is used up in the game.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_bar.note1: A bar of very pure hafnium.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_bar.note2: Crude hafnium + iodine + tungsten wire (iodide process).
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_bar.note3: The same method as zirconium: hafnium iodide splits on the hot wire, leaving pure metal. Hafnium absorbs neutrons well, so it is used in nuclear reactor control rods.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_bar.note4: Zirconium (hardly absorbs neutrons) and hafnium (absorbs them strongly) are almost identical chemically, yet play opposite roles inside a reactor.
item.semiconductor-lab.hafnium_bar.place: Approximation: the vacuum vessel, heating the wire to about 1400 °C and days of growth are left out. Iodine is reused in the real process but one is used up in the game.
item.semiconductor-lab.spent_bayer_liquo: Liquor left after making alumina. Gallium slowly builds up in it.
The Bayer digester puts one out (bottom right) each time the liquor is used up. Gallium cell: 4 of these + a polyethylene bottle → gallium + sodium hydroxide.
Bauxite holds a trace of gallium. Being so like aluminium, it does not settle with aluminium hydroxide and accumulates as the liquor is recycled.
Most of the world's gallium today is recovered this way from alumina-plant liquor.
Omitted: ⚠️ real liquor holds only 0.1–0.2 g of gallium per litre and is concentrated by ion exchange before electrolysis.
item.semiconductor-lab.gallium.note1: A metal that melts in your hand. Material for LEDs.
item.semiconductor-lab.gallium.note2: Gallium cell: 4 spent Bayer liquor + empty polyethylene bottle → this. Material for LEDs ([B-07]).
item.semiconductor-lab.gallium.note3: Melts at about 30 °C. On aluminium it creeps between the crystals and makes it crumble (liquid-metal embrittlement), so it is kept in polyethylene, not metal or glass.
item.semiconductor-lab.gallium.note4: Mendeleev predicted 'eka-aluminium', properties and all, in 1871; Lecoq de Boisbaudran found it in 1875 from spectral lines of zinc blende — a triumph of the periodic table.
block.semiconductor-lab.gallium_cell.not: Electrolyses gallium out of spent alumina-plant liquor.
1 kW. 4 spent Bayer liquor + empty polyethylene bottle → gallium (bottled) + 1 sodium hydroxide (back to the Bayer process). 20 s.
Gallate ions in the alkaline liquor are reduced to metal at a stainless-steel cathode; the liquid gallium pools at the bottom.
The liquor is recycled, so the more alumina you make, the more gallium you get.
block.semiconductor-lab.gallium_cell.pla: Omitted: ⚠️ the ion-exchange concentration step is omitted. Amounts, power and time are game values.
item.semiconductor-lab.white_arsenic.not: A white powder that collects in the flue dust when metal ores are roasted. Highly toxic. ⚠️ Skull symbol
The reverberatory furnace puts one in the by-product slot for every 4 pyrite roasted. Heated with carbon it gives arsenic (an LED material). Industrial material only.
As2O3. Arsenic in the ore turns to fumes on roasting and settles as white powder in the cool flue. GHS: skull (acute toxicity), health hazard (carcinogen), environment (toxic to aquatic life).
Smelter fumes once badly harmed surrounding land and people (mine pollution). Today they must be captured in the flue and not released.
Stone with yellow-brown grains. An ore of cerium and other rare earths.
Rare in Overworld stone (height -16 to 64). Mine with a pickaxe for bastnäsite.
(Ce,La)CO3F. It forms in carbonatite (carbonate rock) deposits. It is said to carry little radioactive thorium, and cerium is its main rare earth.
Mountain Pass in the US and Bayan Obo in China are big mines of this ore.
Approximation: a rare ore in stone in the game (really carbonatite deposits).
block.semiconductor-lab.ion_adsorption_c: Whitish clay with rare earths stuck to it. Rich in yttrium.
Near the surface in jungles and savannas (where bauxite is). Dig with a shovel. 4 + ammonium sulfate + water -> rare-earth leach liquor.

In warm, rainy places, granite weathers into clay with rare-earth ions stuck on the surface (ion adsorption). Washing it with salt water swaps them for ammonium ions and they come out. It carries very little radioactivity.
Deposits in southern China (Jiangxi and others) supply most heavy rare earths such as yttrium. Some mining methods have polluted hills and rivers.
Approximation: really the liquid is soaked through the clay where it lies (in-situ leaching). In the game, a crafting table.
item.semiconductor-lab.bastnaesite.note1: A stone containing the rare earths cerium and lanthanum.
item.semiconductor-lab.bastnaesite.note2: Mined from bastnäsite ore. Roast in a furnace -> roasted bastnäsite.
item.semiconductor-lab.bastnaesite.note3: (Ce,La)CO3F, named after the Bastnäs mine in Sweden, where cerium itself was found in 1803.
item.semiconductor-lab.bastnaesite.note4: 'Rare' earths are not so rare: cerium is about as common in the crust as copper. Rich deposits are few, and separating them is hard.
item.semiconductor-lab.roasted_bastnaesi: Bastnäsite roasted to change its cerium.
Roast bastnäsite in a furnace. + 2 hydrochloric acid -> cerium oxide (the other rare earths dissolve and stay in the grid as light rare-earth liquor).
Roasting in air drives off carbonate and fluorine, and only cerium becomes +4 as CeO2. The other rare earths (+3) dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid but CeO2 does not, so they separate.
Cerium's ability to reach +4 is unusual among rare earths, and separation uses it.
item.semiconductor-lab.cerium_oxide.note: A pale yellow powder. A material for white-LED phosphor.
Roasted bastnäsite + 2 hydrochloric acid (bottles returned). A material for the white-LED phosphor YAG:Ce (E).
CeO2. It is also the polishing powder for glass and lenses ([7-03]). A little in YAG (yttrium aluminium garnet) absorbs blue light and glows yellow.
It is also in lighter flints (ferrocerium) and in car exhaust catalysts.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxalic_acid.note1: White crystalline acid. Used to settle out rare earths.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxalic_acid.note2: Sugar + 2 nitric acid (bottles returned). Rare-earth leach liquor + this -> rare-earth oxalate. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (swallowed, skin).
item.semiconductor-lab.oxalic_acid.note3: Oxidizing sugar with strong nitric acid gives (COOH)2 (Scheele, 1776). Rare-earth oxalates do not dissolve in water, so they settle out of the liquor.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxalic_acid.note4: The bitter taste of spinach is oxalic acid too.
item.semiconductor-lab.oxalic_acid.place: Approximation: the nitrogen dioxide given off is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.rare_earth_leacha: Liquor washed out of the clay, carrying rare earths.
4 ion-adsorption clay + ammonium sulfate + water (bucket returned). + oxalic acid -> rare-earth oxalate.
NH4+ swaps places with the rare-earth ions (RE3+) on the clay surface and they come into the liquid (ion exchange).
The clay stays behind; in reality the liquid is soaked into the hillside and collected below.
item.semiconductor-lab.rare_earth_oxalat: Rare-earth leach liquor + oxalic acid. Roast in a furnace -> rare-earth oxide.
RE2(C2O4)3. Roasting drives off CO and CO2, leaving the oxide.
Precipitating separates the rare earths from aluminium and others in the liquor.
item.semiconductor-lab.mixed_rare_earth_: White powder still mixed with many rare earths. Rich in yttrium.
Roast rare-earth oxalate in a furnace. 4 + hydrochloric acid + cation exchange resin -> 2 yttrium oxide.

Rare earths are so alike that ordinary chemistry can hardly separate them. In 1947 Spedding at the Ames Laboratory in the US ran them through ion-exchange resin columns and separated them by tiny differences in how strongly they stick.
Today they are separated by solvent extraction, shuttling between an organic liquid and water hundreds of times.
item.semiconductor-lab.yttrium_oxide.not: White powder. A material for white-LED phosphor.
4 mixed rare-earth oxide + hydrochloric acid (bottle returned) + cation exchange resin -> 2. A material for the white-LED phosphor YAG:Ce (E).
Y2O3. Fired with aluminium oxide it becomes YAG (Y3Al5O12, a garnet). It was also in the red phosphor (with europium) of old CRT televisions.
Yttrium is named after the Swedish village of Ytterby, whose rocks gave four elements: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.
item.semiconductor-lab.yttrium_oxide.pla: Approximation: ⚠️ the eluting liquid (really citrate or EDTA) is omitted and the resin is used up. The other rare earths are not used.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_die.note1: A steel die that presses metal powder into shape. Reusable.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_die.note2: 8 steel -> 1. In a crafting table with 4 metal powder it makes a green compact (the die is returned). Iron powder -> iron compact; NdFeB powder -> magnet compact.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_die.note3: Powder pressed hard from above and below in the die interlocks into a 'green compact' that holds its shape. It is still fragile; only firing (sintering) makes it strong.
item.semiconductor-lab.steel_die.note4: Powder metallurgy can shape metals that hardly melt (tungsten) and combinations that will not mix when molten. Many gears in cars are made this way.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_powder.note1: Fine iron powder. Pressed and fired, it becomes parts.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_powder.note2: Magnetite + 2 hydrogen (bags) -> 2. 4 + steel die -> iron compact.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_powder.note3: Fe3O4 + 4H2 -> 3Fe + 4H2O. Reduced without melting, the iron comes out porous like a sponge and crumbles into powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_powder.note4: In 1910 Höganäs in Sweden began making sponge-iron powder by reducing iron ore without melting it.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_powder.place: Approximation: Höganäs reduced with coke; the water given off is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.iron_compact.note: 4 iron powder + steel die (returned). Sinter in the electric furnace -> sintered gear.
The grains only interlock and are not joined yet. When fired, atoms move where grains touch and grow necks between them (sintering).
Sintered parts can soak oil into their pores to become self-lubricating bearings.
item.semiconductor-lab.sintered_gear.not: A gear made by firing iron powder.
Fire an iron compact in the electric furnace. A machine part.
Fired at about 1100 °C, below iron's melting point (about 1540 °C), it keeps the die's shape and needs no machining (near-net shape).
In 1955 the Battelle laboratory in the US built hot isostatic pressing (HIP), squeezing parts equally from all sides at high temperature to close the pores (ASME landmark).
item.semiconductor-lab.sintered_gear.pla: Approximation: the sintering atmosphere (hydrogen or other reducing gas) and HIP are omitted (explained only).
item.semiconductor-lab.light_rare_earth_: Liquor left after removing cerium, with lanthanum, neodymium and others dissolved.
Left in the crafting grid when roasted bastnäsite + 2 hydrochloric acid makes cerium oxide. + oxalic acid -> oxalate.
The +3 rare earths (lanthanum, praseodymium, neodymium) are dissolved as chlorides in the dilute acid; only CeO2 stays undissolved.
Neodymium is only 10-20% of bastnäsite's rare earths, yet as a strong-magnet material it is worth more than cerium.
A white precipitate of lanthanum, neodymium and others.
Light rare-earth liquor + oxalic acid. Roast in a furnace -> light rare-earth oxide.
RE2(C2O4)3. Precipitating with oxalic acid separates them from everything else in the liquor.
Powder of light rare earths still mixed.
Roast light rare-earth oxalate in a furnace. 4 + hydrochloric acid + cation exchange resin -> neodymium oxide.
La, Pr and Nd are neighbouring elements with near-identical behaviour; they are separated by tiny differences in how they stick to ion-exchange resin (as with Y).
Praseodymium and neodymium were once thought to be one element, 'didymium' (Welsbach split it in 1885).
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium_oxide.n: A pale violet powder. The starting point for neodymium magnets.
4 light rare-earth oxide + hydrochloric acid (bottle returned) + cation exchange resin -> 1. + 2 hydrofluoric acid -> neodymium fluoride.
Nd2O3. Neodymium ions absorb particular colours of light, so it looks pale violet (and changes shade under different lights).
Neodymium glass absorbs the glaring sodium-yellow light of hot glass, so glassblowers' goggles use it.
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium_oxide.p: Approximation: ⚠️ the eluting liquid is omitted and the resin is used up. Lanthanum and praseodymium are not used.
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium_fluorid: Neodymium and fluorine powder. Melted and electrolysed.
Neodymium oxide + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned). Neodymium oxide + this + graphite rod -> electrolysis charge. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity.
Nd2O3 + 6HF -> 2NdF3 + 3H2O. Dissolving Nd2O3 in molten NdF3 and passing current gives neodymium metal.
The same idea as getting aluminium from alumina dissolved in cryolite (Hall-Héroult).
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium_electro: Material that becomes neodymium metal when melted and electrolysed.
Neodymium oxide + neodymium fluoride + graphite rod. Electric furnace -> neodymium.
In fluoride melted at about 1050 °C, oxygen leaves at the graphite anode as CO and CO2, and neodymium collects at the cathode (molten-salt electrolysis).
Neodymium corrodes quickly in water, so it cannot be won by electrolysing a water solution.
Approximation: ⚠️ the electric furnace simply yields metal (really a dedicated cell electrolysing molten salt).
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium.note1: A silvery rare-earth metal that tarnishes easily in air.
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium.note2: Electrolysis charge in the electric furnace. 2 + 4 iron powder + ferroboron -> NdFeB alloy.
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium.note3: Nd. Since it corrodes easily, it is normally used as an alloy with iron and boron.
item.semiconductor-lab.neodymium.note4: The name means 'new twin' (the new half split from didymium, 'twin').
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron_charge: A mix of boron oxide, iron ore and charcoal.
Boron trioxide + magnetite + 2 charcoal. Blast furnace -> ferroboron.
Carbon reduces boron oxide and iron oxide together into an iron-boron alloy (carbothermic reduction).
Making an alloy with iron is far easier than isolating boron itself.
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron.note1: An iron-boron alloy. Puts the boron into neodymium magnets.
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron.note2: Ferroboron charge in a blast furnace. A material for NdFeB alloy.
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron.note3: An iron alloy with about 18% boron. A little in steel makes it harden more easily.
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron.note4: The B (boron) in the magnet's Nd2Fe14B is only about 1% by weight.
item.semiconductor-lab.ferroboron.placeh: Approximation: the boron fraction is not tracked.
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_alloy.note1: An alloy of neodymium, iron and boron. Turned into powder, then magnets.
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_alloy.note2: 2 neodymium + 4 iron powder + ferroboron. + hydrogen -> 2 NdFeB powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_alloy.note3: Crystals of Nd2Fe14B. Among the many iron atoms, neodymium locks the magnetic direction strongly along one axis (magnetic anisotropy).
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_alloy.note4: In reality the molten alloy is splashed onto a spinning copper wheel to cool it fast into thin flakes (strip casting).
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_alloy.place: Approximation: melting and rapid cooling are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_powder.note: Very fine powder of neodymium-magnet alloy.
NdFeB alloy + hydrogen (bag) -> 2. 4 + steel die + magnetizing yoke -> compact. ⚠ Burns easily in air.
The alloy absorbs hydrogen, swells, cracks and falls apart (hydrogen decrepitation). It is milled further so each grain is a single crystal (a few micrometres).
Such fine powder can catch fire in air, so factories handle it under nitrogen.
A tool that makes a strong field with an electromagnet, lining up and magnetizing magnets.
4 steel + electromagnet. Returned after crafting. Used when pressing NdFeB powder and to magnetize after sintering.
A field while pressing lines up the grains' magnetic directions (alignment). After sintering, an even stronger field turns the whole piece into one magnet (magnetization).
Real magnetizers dump the charge of capacitors all at once to make a very strong field for an instant.
item.semiconductor-lab.ndfeb_compact.not: A block of magnet powder pressed in a magnetic field.
4 NdFeB powder + steel die + magnetizing yoke (both returned). Sinter in the electric furnace -> sintered NdFeB.
The grains are fixed with their magnetic directions aligned. Still fragile; firing removes the pores and hardens it.
Without alignment, the same material makes a much weaker magnet.
item.semiconductor-lab.sintered_ndfeb.no: Fired magnet material. Not yet a magnet.
Fire an NdFeB compact in the electric furnace. + magnetizing yoke (returned) -> neodymium magnet.
Sintered at about 1050 °C, a thin neodymium-rich layer forms between the grains and cuts their magnetic interference - the secret of its strength.
Real magnets corrode easily, so they are nickel-plated ([2-50] plating).
item.semiconductor-lab.sintered_ndfeb.pl: Approximation: post-sintering heat treatment and plating are omitted.
The strongest permanent magnet. Used in linear motors, phone speakers and electric-car motors.
Sintered NdFeB + magnetizing yoke (returned). A material for the EUV scanner's stage (linear motor [8-09]).
Nd2Fe14B. For the same size it is about ten times as strong as old ferrite magnets, so motors can be small and light.

Invented in 1982-84 almost simultaneously by researchers at Sumitomo Special Metals in Japan (sintered) and GM in the US (rapidly quenched). It weakens with heat (above about 80 °C), so hot motors add a little dysprosium.
item.semiconductor-lab.vanadium_magnetit: Black grains in iron sand carrying a little vanadium.
Rarely (8%) found when digging iron sand on beaches. 2 + salt -> roast charge.
Magnetite with some iron replaced by vanadium and titanium (titanomagnetite). Most of the world's vanadium today comes from such iron ores as a by-product of iron-making.
Japanese iron sand also contains vanadium, said to be one reason tatara steel is strong ⚠️.
Approximation: really often taken from iron-making slag (vanadium slag). In the game a by-product of iron sand (decision Q3-18 ①).
item.semiconductor-lab.vanadium_roast_ch: 2 vanadium-bearing magnetite + salt. Roast in a furnace -> calcine.
Roasting with salt in air turns vanadium into water-soluble sodium vanadate NaVO3 (salt roasting); iron stays as insoluble oxide.
Because chlorine-bearing gas comes off, many plants now roast with sodium carbonate instead.
Ore roasted so its vanadium dissolves in water.
Roast charge from the furnace. + water (bucket returned) -> sodium vanadate solution.
Sodium vanadate dissolves while iron oxide stays behind, so washing with water takes out only the vanadium (leaching).
The leftover iron oxide can go back to iron-making.
Approximation: the roasting temperature (about 850 °C) is omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_vanadate_s: A yellowish solution with dissolved vanadium.
Vanadium calcine + water. + ammonium chloride -> ammonium metavanadate.
NaVO3 in solution. Vanadium compounds turn yellow, blue, green or violet depending on oxidation state.
Vanadium is named after Vanadís, the Norse goddess of beauty, for the beauty of its compounds' colours.
item.semiconductor-lab.ammonium_metavana: Sodium vanadate solution + ammonium chloride. Roast in a furnace -> vanadium pentoxide. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity.
NaVO3 + NH4Cl -> NH4VO3 (precipitate) + NaCl. It barely dissolves, so it settles out. Roasting drives off ammonia and water, leaving V2O5.
Precipitate then roast - the same idea as the rare-earth oxalates.
item.semiconductor-lab.vanadium_pentoxid: An orange powder. A catalyst that oxidizes things with air.
Roast ammonium metavanadate in a furnace. Returned after crafting (a catalyst). Naphthalene + this -> phthalic anhydride. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (inhalation), suspected mutagen and carcinogen.
V2O5 hands over oxygen and becomes V2O4, then air turns it back into V2O5. Repeating this, a little drives a lot of reaction.
In the contact process for sulfuric acid [6-13], V2O5 replaced expensive platinum as the catalyst from the 1910s-20s.
Approximation: real catalysts slowly weaken; in the game it is not used up.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron_magnesium_m: A powder for freeing boron. Fire it in a blast furnace.
Crafting: 1 boron oxide + 3 magnesium. Blast it for crude boron.
B2O3 + 3Mg → 2B + 3MgO. Magnesium grabs oxygen so strongly that it strips it from boron.
The reaction is violent and hot (a thermite-type reaction); plants do it in small batches in closed vessels.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_boron.note1: Boron powder mixed with magnesium oxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_boron.note2: Blast the mix. Washing with hydrochloric acid dissolves the magnesium oxide and leaves boron.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_boron.note3: Moissan made boron of about 90% purity this way in 1892.
item.semiconductor-lab.crude_boron.note4: Purer boron is made by reducing boron trichloride with hydrogen (2BCl3 + 3H2 → 2B + 6HCl).
item.semiconductor-lab.boron.note1: A dark, very hard element — the source of p-type silicon.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron.note2: Crude boron + hydrochloric acid (crafting) → this (the magnesium oxide becomes magnesium chloride and washes away; the bottle comes back).
item.semiconductor-lab.boron.note3: Boron has one electron fewer, so in silicon it leaves a hole and makes it p-type. The game's dopant source uses easier-to-handle boron oxide.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron.note4: Used in boron carbide, the hardest material after diamond, and in reactor control rods that absorb neutrons.
item.semiconductor-lab.boron.placeholder: Omitted: ⚠️ about 90% purity (Moissan's method). High-purity BCl3 hydrogen reduction is not made.
item.semiconductor-lab.native_copper.not: Copper that comes out of the ground already as metal. It can be hammered into shape.
Sometimes drops when mining copper ore (5% ⚠️). Smelt it for a copper ingot.
Hammering hardens it (work hardening); heating softens it again (annealing). One of the first metals people used.
Beads hammered from native copper around 8000 BC have been found in Anatolia (modern Turkey); big lumps came from around North America's Great Lakes.
block.semiconductor-lab.magnesium_cell.h: Put in anhydrous magnesium chloride and connect power. Out come magnesium and a chlorine bag. Dry the bittern salt first.
block.semiconductor-lab.bayer_digester.h: Insert bauxite, sodium hydroxide and a water bucket → aluminium hydroxide and red mud. 2 kW. Every 4 uses of the liquor, spent liquor (gallium) appears bottom right.
block.semiconductor-lab.castner_cell.how: Insert 4 sodium hydroxide and an empty iron flask → metallic sodium. 2 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.gallium_cell.how: Insert 4 spent Bayer liquor and an empty polyethylene bottle → gallium and sodium hydroxide. 1 kW.
block.semiconductor-lab.hall_heroult_cel: Insert alumina, cryolite and graphite rods (anodes) → aluminium. Needs a lot of power. Anodes wear away.
block.semiconductor-lab.tantalum_refiner: Tantalite + 2 hydrofluoric acid + potassium fluoride → K2TaF7; that + metallic sodium → tantalum. 3 kW. Containers pop out.
